demographics: Inguinal hernia is far more common in men; umbilical and incisional hernias are more evenly distributed between sexes
Risk rises with age as abdominal wall strength declines
Umbilical hernias are common in infants and often close on their own
Incisional hernia follows prior abdominal surgery

risk_factors.text: Chronic straining from heavy lifting or constipation

comorbidities: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with straining to urinate
family_history: Hernia in a parent or sibling
social_history: Occupations or hobbies involving heavy lifting

chief_complaints.text: I have a bulge in my groin
It hurts when I lift things or cough
I feel a heavy, dragging feeling down there

hpi.onset: Gradual; noticed incidentally or after straining, lifting, coughing or standing for a long time
hpi.duration: Weeks to years; often present for months before evaluation
hpi.progression: Slowly enlarges over time; may intermittently reduce when lying down and reappear with standing, coughing or straining
hpi.location: Groin or scrotum (inguinal), around the umbilicus (umbilical), or at a prior surgical scar (incisional)
hpi.radiation: Discomfort may radiate to the groin, scrotum or inner thigh; usually no true radiation
hpi.quality: A soft, reducible swelling with a dull ache, heaviness or dragging sensation
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; often 2–5/10, worse with activity
hpi.timing: Intermittent; worse with standing, straining, lifting, coughing or at the end of the day, better when lying down
relieving: Gentle pressure pushing the bulge back in

associated_symptoms.text: A visible or palpable bulge that reduces when lying down
Aching or dragging discomfort in the groin or abdomen
Bulge gets bigger with coughing or straining

pertinent_negatives: Severe constant pain with a firm, tender, irreducible lump (suggests incarceration or strangulation)
Vomiting and inability to pass gas or stool (suggests obstruction)
Fever with an overlying red, warm skin (suggests strangulation)
Blood in stool or black stools

negatives: Inability to pass gas or stool

positives.text: Groin or abdominal wall discomfort with activity

atypical.how_it_differs: Umbilical and inguinal hernias are common in infants and young children; many umbilical hernias close spontaneously by age 4–5, and the child may have no pain at all.
May present with vague abdominal or groin discomfort without a clearly visible bulge, especially if obese; risk of incarceration is higher and symptoms may be attributed to other conditions.
Increased intra-abdominal pressure can worsen or reveal umbilical and inguinal hernias; the gravid uterus can mask the bulge and symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy discomfort.
A thick abdominal wall can hide the bulge, so the patient may report only pain or a pressure sensation; imaging may be needed to confirm the hernia.

general.mild: Comfortable, well-appearing, no distress; able to stand and move normally
general.moderate: Mild discomfort with movement or straining; otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, guarding the area, reluctant to move or strain, may be tachycardic
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, lying still with a rigid tender abdomen; signs of shock or obstruction

findings.maneuver: Inspect the groin, umbilicus and prior scars with the patient standing and then supine
findings.finding: A visible soft swelling or bulge that is more prominent when standing and may disappear when lying down

findings.maneuver: Palpate the swelling gently and attempt to reduce it with steady pressure
findings.finding: A soft, smooth, reducible mass that returns into the abdomen with gentle pressure

findings.maneuver: Place a finger at the superficial inguinal ring and ask the patient to cough
findings.finding: A palpable impulse or expansion of the bulge with coughing or straining

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough while palpating the swelling
findings.finding: The swelling expands outward with the cough (expansile impulse)

findings.maneuver: Invaginate the scrotal skin and palpate the superficial inguinal ring
findings.finding: A widened, patulous superficial inguinal ring

findings.maneuver: Palpate the umbilicus and surrounding abdominal wall
findings.finding: A fascial defect or soft swelling at the umbilicus

findings.maneuver: Palpate along any prior abdominal surgical scar while the patient lifts the head or coughs
findings.finding: A fascial defect or bulge at the scar site

findings.maneuver: Attempt to reduce the swelling with gentle pressure
findings.finding: A firm, tender, irreducible mass that cannot be pushed back

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the swelling
findings.finding: Erythema, warmth, induration or discoloration over the hernia

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and assess for guarding and rebound tenderness
findings.finding: Guarding, rigidity or rebound tenderness suggesting peritoneal irritation

findings.maneuver: Auscultate bowel sounds in all quadrants
findings.finding: High-pitched or absent bowel sounds suggesting obstruction

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen away from the hernia
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Palpate both testes and the scrotum
findings.finding: Normal testes without a separate scrotal mass or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal and femoral lymph nodes
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the femoral canal just below the inguinal ligament

labs.caveat: Normal in an uncomplicated, reducible hernia. Leukocytosis with a left shift suggests strangulation or bowel ischemia and should prompt urgent surgery.
Left shift accompanies leukocytosis in strangulation.
Elevated lactate with an irreducible, tender hernia suggests strangulated bowel with ischemia; a normal value does not exclude it.
Rises with vomiting and dehydration from obstruction.
Pre-renal azotemia from vomiting and poor intake in obstruction.
Negative. Ordered in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or surgery; a positive result changes the imaging and operative plan.

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the groin or abdominal wall
imaging.preferred_when: Children, pregnancy, and when the diagnosis is uncertain on exam

findings.text: A fascial defect with a soft-tissue or bowel-containing sac that changes with Valsalva or standing
Reducible hernia contents with no surrounding inflammation
No hernia identified (nondiagnostic, especially with a small or occult defect)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Obese patients, occult or recurrent hernia, suspected incarceration or obstruction, or when the diagnosis is unclear

findings.text: Fascial defect with herniation of bowel, omentum or fat
Dilated fluid-filled bowel loops with a transition point (obstruction)
Bowel wall thickening, poor enhancement or mesenteric stranding suggesting strangulation
Free air or fluid suggesting perforation
Usually normal in a simple, reducible hernia
Dilated air-filled bowel loops with air-fluid levels suggesting obstruction
Free air under the diaphragm suggesting perforation

imaging.preferred_when: Symptoms of reflux or dysphagia suggesting a hiatal hernia

findings.text: Retroflexed view showing a widened hiatus with gastric folds above the diaphragm
Esophagitis or a peptic stricture from reflux

imaging.study: Barium swallow or upper gastrointestinal series
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected hiatal hernia or when endoscopy is not available

findings.text: Contrast-filled pouch of stomach above the diaphragm
Reflux of contrast into the esophagus

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis suggesting strangulation or infection
Assesses hydration, electrolytes and renal function if vomiting or obstruction

initial.test: Ultrasound of the groin or abdominal wall
initial.why: Confirms the hernia and assesses contents without radiation
initial.only_if: the diagnosis is uncertain on exam, or the patient is a child or pregnant

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before imaging or surgery

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Defines the anatomy and detects incarceration, obstruction or strangulation
confirmatory.only_if: the diagnosis is unclear, the patient is obese, or a complication is suspected

supporting.why: Supports bowel ischemia when strangulation is suspected
Screens for obstruction or free air
supporting.only_if: vomiting, distension or inability to pass gas or stool

supporting.why: Evaluates reflux symptoms and confirms a hiatal hernia

not_indicated.why: No role in evaluating a hernia
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatic disease is suspected
Not routinely needed; consider only if urinary symptoms suggest another cause

decision_points: A firm, tender, irreducible hernia with systemic signs is an emergency and goes to surgery without delay
Pregnancy test before CT or surgery in anyone who could be pregnant
Ultrasound first in children and pregnancy; CT if the diagnosis remains unclear
Vomiting, distension and inability to pass gas or stool suggest obstruction and need urgent surgical evaluation

differential.name: Femoral hernia
differential.why_considered: Groin bulge with pain, especially in a woman or an older adult
differential.trigger: A groin bulge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, or a woman with a painful groin lump

history: Bulge located lower in the groin, just below the inguinal ligament
Often smaller and less reducible than an inguinal hernia
Higher risk of incarceration and strangulation
exam: Mass below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, medial to the femoral vessels
No impulse with coughing in many cases
imaging: Ultrasound or CT showing a defect in the femoral canal with herniated contents

differential.name: Inguinal lymphadenopathy
differential.why_considered: A lump in the groin that can be mistaken for a hernia

history: Recent infection, injury or vaccination in the leg or groin
No positional change with standing or lying down
exam: Firm, discrete, often tender lymph nodes
labs: May show signs of infection if due to a local source
imaging: Ultrasound showing enlarged lymph nodes without a fascial defect

differential.name: Hydrocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal or groin swelling that can mimic an inguinal hernia

history: Painless scrotal swelling that does not reduce with lying down
No association with straining or coughing
exam: Testis may be difficult to palpate separately
imaging: Ultrasound showing a fluid collection around the testis with no bowel in the scrotum

differential.name: Varicocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling or discomfort that can be confused with a hernia

history: Dull scrotal ache, often worse with standing and at the end of the day
exam: Bag of worms texture above the testis
Worse with standing and Valsalva, improves when lying down
No fascial defect or bowel in the scrotum
imaging: Ultrasound showing dilated veins in the pampiniform plexus

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute scrotal or groin pain that can be mistaken for an incarcerated hernia
differential.trigger: Sudden severe testicular pain with nausea and vomiting, especially in a young male

history: Sudden onset of severe testicular pain
No history of a reducible bulge
exam: Severe tenderness of the testis itself
imaging: Doppler ultrasound showing reduced or absent blood flow to the testis

differential.name: Epididymitis
differential.why_considered: Scrotal pain and swelling that can mimic a hernia

labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia or gonorrhea
imaging: Ultrasound showing an enlarged, hyperemic epididymis with normal testicular flow

differential.name: Psoas abscess
differential.why_considered: Groin or flank pain with a mass that can be mistaken for a hernia
differential.trigger: Fever, back or flank pain, and a limp or inability to extend the hip

exam: Tenderness in the flank or iliac fossa
imaging: CT or MRI showing a fluid collection in the psoas muscle

differential.name: Abdominal wall hematoma
differential.why_considered: A painful abdominal wall mass that can resemble a hernia

history: Recent trauma, coughing fit or anticoagulant use
No history of a longstanding bulge
exam: Tender, firm mass that does not reduce
imaging: Ultrasound or CT showing a fluid collection within the abdominal wall muscles without a fascial defect

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Heartburn and regurgitation that can be caused by a hiatal hernia or mimic its symptoms

history: Symptoms worse when lying down or bending over
imaging: Endoscopy may show esophagitis or a hiatal hernia
Barium swallow may show reflux or a hiatal hernia

severity.mild: Small, reducible hernia with minimal or no pain; no signs of obstruction or strangulation
severity.moderate: Larger or symptomatic hernia with activity-related pain and a reducible bulge; no systemic signs
severity.severe: Incarcerated hernia: irreducible, tender bulge, may have nausea or vomiting, but no signs of bowel ischemia or peritonitis
severity.critical: Strangulated hernia with bowel ischemia, obstruction or perforation; systemic toxicity, hemodynamic instability or peritonitis

red_flags.finding: Overlying erythema, warmth or skin discoloration
red_flags.meaning: Strangulation with tissue ischemia; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Vomiting, abdominal distension and inability to pass gas or stool

red_flags.meaning: Strangulation with sepsis or bowel ischemia

complications.name: Strangulation with bowel ischemia
clues: Severe pain out of proportion to exam

complications.name: Bowel obstruction
clues: Inability to pass gas or stool

complications.name: Recurrence after repair
clues: Bulge reappears at the same site months to years after surgery
Often associated with chronic straining or wound infection

special_populations.differences: Umbilical hernias are common in infants and often close spontaneously by age 4–5; inguinal hernias in children are usually congenital and have a high risk of incarceration, so they are repaired promptly. Ultrasound is preferred over CT.
Higher risk of incarceration and strangulation; symptoms may be vague and the bulge may be hidden by obesity. Comorbidities increase operative risk.

Increased intra-abdominal pressure can worsen or reveal umbilical and inguinal hernias; the gravid uterus can mask the bulge. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging; surgery is generally deferred until after delivery unless complications occur.
A thick abdominal wall can hide the bulge, so patients may report only pain or pressure. Imaging is often needed to confirm the diagnosis, and weight loss is recommended before elective repair.

key_questions.question: Where exactly do you feel the bulge or discomfort?
key_questions.looking_for: Groin or scrotum (inguinal), around the umbilicus (umbilical), or at a prior surgical scar (incisional)

key_questions.question: Does the lump come and go, and does it change when you stand up or lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: A reducible bulge that is more prominent with standing or straining and disappears when lying down

key_questions.question: What brings it out or makes it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy lifting, coughing, straining with bowel movements or urination, prolonged standing

key_questions.question: How long has it been there, and is it getting bigger?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months with slow enlargement

key_questions.question: Can you push it back in, or has it ever gotten stuck?
key_questions.looking_for: A bulge that is usually reducible; a stuck, irreducible lump suggests incarceration

key_questions.question: Is the pain sharp and constant, or more of a dull ache or heaviness?
key_questions.looking_for: Dull ache or dragging sensation; severe constant pain suggests strangulation

key_questions.question: Have you had any vomiting, abdominal swelling, or trouble passing gas or stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of bowel obstruction from an incarcerated hernia

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills?
Have you had any abdominal or groin surgery in the past?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery raises the possibility of an incisional hernia

key_questions.question: Do you have a chronic cough, constipation, or trouble urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that cause chronic straining and raise intra-abdominal pressure

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a hernia?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of hernia or connective tissue problems

key_questions.question: Does your work or hobbies involve heavy lifting?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or recreational straining that contributes to the hernia

key_questions.question: Do you smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking with chronic cough, a risk factor for hernia

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any blood in your stool or black stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Bleeding that would suggest another cause or a complication

key_questions.question: Have you had any unexplained weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight loss that would raise concern for malignancy

reasoning_points: A visible or palpable bulge that is more prominent with standing, coughing or straining and reduces when lying down
A soft, reducible mass with an expansile cough impulse on examination
Risk factors such as male sex, older age, prior surgery, chronic straining, chronic cough or obesity
Absence of systemic signs such as fever, severe constant pain or peritoneal findings in an uncomplicated hernia
Recognition that a firm, tender, irreducible bulge with vomiting or systemic signs suggests incarceration or strangulation and needs urgent surgery
Pregnancy excluded before imaging or surgery when relevant
Imaging reserved for uncertain, occult or complicated cases

easy: Older man with a longstanding reducible groin bulge that appears with standing and coughing
Bulge reduces when lying down and has a positive cough impulse
No pain, fever or obstructive symptoms
medium: Obese patient with groin or abdominal pain but no clearly visible bulge
Umbilical or incisional hernia at a prior surgical scar
Hiatal hernia presenting with heartburn and regurgitation rather than a visible lump
Small hernia with intermittent symptoms and a nondiagnostic exam
hard: Incarcerated hernia with an irreducible, tender bulge and vomiting
Strangulated hernia with overlying skin changes, leukocytosis and elevated lactate
Older adult with vague abdominal discomfort and a hidden hernia
Pregnant patient with an umbilical or inguinal bulge masked by the gravid uterus
Child with an umbilical hernia that may close spontaneously
